latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Rupture of maternal decidual or spiral-artery vessels at the placental bed initiates bleeding between placenta and uterine wall. This is the upstream maternal bleeding driver in placental abruption.
Blood accumulates behind or around the placenta; expansion may be revealed through the cervix or concealed behind the placenta and can mechanically dissect the placenta from the uterus.
Progressive detachment reduces functional placental exchange surface. Larger central or complete separations produce maternal bleeding, uterine irritability, fetal distress, and fetal death.
Retroplacental blood and myometrial irritation cause painful uterine tenderness, frequent contractions, hypertonus, or a board-like tetanic uterus.

Placental detachment and maternal hypoperfusion reduce fetal oxygen and nutrient transfer, producing nonreassuring fetal status, fetal acidemia, reduced movement, fetal anemia in some cases, and fetal death.
Decidual and placental tissue factor enters maternal circulation and, with hemorrhage and shock, can drive rapid hypofibrinogenemia, D-dimer rise, platelet consumption, prolonged PT/aPTT, and DIC.
Visible and concealed maternal blood loss lowers oxygen delivery and perfusion pressure, causing tachycardia, low MAP, rising lactate, oliguria, AKI, shock, and maternal death hazard.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Chronic or recurrent abruption with placental insufficiency
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Small, marginal, or recurrent placental separations may present with intermittent dark bleeding, placental insufficiency, oligohydramnios, growth restriction, and episodic fetal compromise rather than sudden shock.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Maternal decidual vessel bleeding creates the retroplacental clot or concealed hemorrhage.
Expanding blood dissects the placenta from the uterine wall, increasing separation area.
Retroplacental blood and myometrial irritation produce uterine tenderness, irritability, and hypertonus.
Loss of attached placental surface rapidly reduces fetal oxygen transfer.
Large placental bed injury exposes tissue factor and accelerates obstetric consumptive coagulopathy.
Visible or concealed blood loss lowers circulating volume and perfusion.
Recurrent marginal bleeding can intermittently enlarge the detached or infarcted placental region.
Chronic abruption overlaps with placental insufficiency and reduced fetal reserve.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Placental abruption requires a current intrauterine pregnancy context; postpartum bleeding alone belongs to other manifolds.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: The placenta and decidual vascular bed are prerequisite state-space context.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Lower likelihood in fully concealed central abruption.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Blood may track through the decidua and cervix to become visible vaginal bleeding.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: External bleeding may underestimate total blood loss.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Revealed hemorrhage intensity often increases with larger marginal or communicated hematoma.
Chronic abruption often produces intermittent dark brown spotting rather than brisk red bleeding.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Central abruption, intact membranes, or trapped clot can conceal blood.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Shock, pain, and fetal distress may be out of proportion to visible blood loss.
The pathologic clot can sometimes be visualized by ultrasound, MRI, CT, operation, or placental inspection.
Larger concealed clots increase measured thickness when imaging can separate clot from placenta.
Large concealed hematomas can be estimated volumetrically by imaging or intraoperative assessment.
Separation area is the anatomic expression of the abruption.
Blood may enter the amniotic cavity when membranes or the placental edge communicate with the clot.
Myometrial irritation and uterine hypertonus produce acute abdominal pain.
Pain may be severe or constant in moderate to severe abruption.
Acute abruption often begins suddenly with pain or contractions.
Tenderness to uterine palpation is a core physical finding.
The uterus may become markedly tender in concealed or severe abruption.
A firm, hypertonic, board-like uterus reflects myometrial irritability from blood infiltration and tetany.
Tetanic contractions are characteristic of more severe abruption.
Uterine irritability can produce painful contractions or frequent tightening.
Uterine irritability can produce frequent contractions or tachysystole.
Reduced placental oxygen transfer and fetal reserve can reduce perceived fetal movement.
Loss of placental exchange surface causes nonreassuring fetal status.
Fetal hypoxemia may appear as recurrent late decelerations, reduced variability, prolonged deceleration, or category III tracing.
Severe acute placental separation can produce sustained fetal bradycardia.
Uteroplacental insufficiency can generate recurrent late decelerations.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Direction is most relevant for sustained bradycardia; early or milder stress can show tachycardia or decelerations instead.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Severe fetal hypoxia can lower fetal heart rate.
Placental exchange failure directly raises fetal acidemia and hypoxic injury hazard.
Complete or near-complete abruption can cause fetal death rapidly unless delivery occurs in time.
Chronic placental insufficiency associated with abruption can restrict fetal growth.
Reduced placental function can reduce fetal renal perfusion and amniotic fluid.
Placental abruption-associated DIC can consume fibrinogen early; low fibrinogen is a sensitive severity marker in obstetric hemorrhage.
Coagulation activation and fibrinolysis raise D-dimer and fibrin split products.
Consumptive coagulopathy and bleeding can lower platelet count.
Severe consumptive coagulopathy prolongs PT/INR.
Severe consumptive coagulopathy prolongs aPTT.
Placental tissue factor and hemorrhagic shock can transition to overt DIC.
Hypofibrinogenemia and platelet consumption worsen uterine, surgical, and postpartum bleeding.
Maternal blood loss lowers hemoglobin after equilibration or with massive hemorrhage.
Maternal blood loss lowers hematocrit after equilibration or massive hemorrhage.
Compensatory tachycardia is an early sign of hypovolemia.
Severe blood loss causes hypotension and low perfusion pressure.
Heart-rate-to-systolic-pressure ratio rises with occult and overt obstetric hemorrhage.
Hypoperfusion and shock increase lactate.
Renal hypoperfusion produces oliguria.
Severe abruption can cause hemorrhagic shock, including when bleeding is concealed.
Shock and DIC can produce ischemic acute kidney injury.
Abruption and coagulopathy increase postpartum uterine bleeding risk after delivery.
DIC and low fibrinogen increase postpartum hemorrhage after placental delivery.
Abruption often necessitates preterm delivery or triggers labor before term.
Maternal shock is a major proximal driver of death hazard.
DIC and major bleeding increase maternal mortality hazard.
Fetal compromise increases urgency of delivery once fetal viability and maternal status are considered.
Maternal instability makes placental source removal and hemorrhage control urgent.

axes.shape_free_text: Probability that the patient is currently pregnant with an intrauterine gestation; placental abruption is an antepartum placental disease.
axes.required_context_rationale: This disease manifold requires active pregnancy or postpartum/peripartum context; without that context, nonspecific abdominal pain, hypertension, hemolysis, liver injury, fever, or shock should not make it rank high.

axes.shape_free_text: Gestational age when abruption occurs; changes fetal viability, prematurity risk, monitoring, steroid, magnesium, and delivery context.
Probability that the fetus is viable enough for fetal-monitoring and delivery decisions to affect fetal outcome.
Probability that placenta previa has been excluded sufficiently to allow safe cervical assessment or vaginal delivery planning.
Probability that maternal instability, fetal compromise, term gestation, active bleeding, or DIC makes delivery time-critical.
Feasibility and safety of cesarean delivery given maternal stability, coagulopathy, anesthesia, fetal viability, surgical access, and consent context.
Feasibility of vaginal delivery given maternal stability, fetal status, cervical/labor progress, placenta previa exclusion, and contraindications.
Availability of crossmatched or emergency blood products including red cells, plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate, and fibrinogen concentrate.
Probability that the mother is RhD-negative and unsensitized, making RhD immune globulin relevant after antepartum bleeding or fetomaternal hemorrhage.
Availability of neonatal team, NICU, blood gas assessment, transfusion, and respiratory support for a potentially preterm or hypoxic infant.
Visible vaginal bleeding during the second half of pregnancy.
Amount or clinical severity of visible vaginal bleeding when present.
Dark brown or old vaginal blood, more typical of chronic or recurrent abruption than brisk acute bleeding.
Probability that significant blood is trapped behind the placenta or within the uterus, so visible bleeding underestimates total blood loss.
Acute abdominal pain in pregnancy from uterine bleeding, contractions, or hypertonus.
Severity of abdominal pain when present; can be severe and constant in concealed or severe abruption.
Sudden onset of pain rather than slowly progressive discomfort.
Tenderness of the gravid uterus to palpation.
Degree of uterine tenderness when present.
Firm, hypertonic, board-like uterus between contractions.
Tetanic uterine contraction or persistent rigid uterine tone when hypertonus is present.
Painful, frequent, or otherwise clinically notable uterine contractions.
Frequency of contractions or uterine irritability on exam or tocodynamometry.
Retroplacental, subchorionic, marginal, or intra-placental hematoma seen on imaging, operation, or placental inspection.

Estimated percent of placental attachment separated or nonfunctional when reported by imaging, operation, pathology, or clinical adjudication.

Maternal report of decreased or absent fetal movement.
Clinical or monitoring evidence of fetal compromise.
Nonreassuring electronic fetal heart tracing such as reduced variability, recurrent decelerations, prolonged deceleration, sinusoidal pattern, or category III tracing.
Sustained fetal bradycardia in a viable monitored pregnancy.
Recurrent late decelerations on fetal heart monitoring.
Fetal heart rate in beats per minute when a viable fetus is being monitored.

Maternal aPTT; may prolong in severe DIC or massive transfusion.

Maternal heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure; rises in occult or overt hemorrhagic shock.
Maternal serum lactate from tissue hypoperfusion.
Maternal urine output; falls with renal hypoperfusion, shock, or DIC.
Near-term probability of hemorrhagic shock from visible or concealed abruption bleeding.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Weaker when hemorrhage is fully concealed or labs are drawn before equilibration.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: More visible bleeding generally lowers hemoglobin, but visible bleeding may underestimate total blood loss.
Concealed bleeding allows shock to be more severe than visible blood loss suggests.
Pain out of proportion to visible bleeding increases concern for concealed retroplacental hemorrhage.
Uterine hypertonus reflects severe myometrial/placental irritation and reduced uteroplacental perfusion.
Larger separation removes placental exchange surface and sharply increases fetal acidemia risk.
Persistent fetal compromise can progress to fetal death if the placental state is not reversed by delivery.
Low fibrinogen is a major driver of uncontrolled obstetric bleeding.
Rapid hypofibrinogenemia marks overt obstetric consumptive coagulopathy.
Thrombocytopenia adds surgical and obstetric bleeding risk when DIC or hypertensive overlap is present.
Maternal hypotension reduces uteroplacental perfusion and worsens fetal status.
Lactate reflects severity of maternal hypoperfusion and shock.
Uncontrolled hemorrhagic shock is the main acute maternal fatal pathway.
DIC increases fatal hemorrhage, organ failure, and operative bleeding.
Uncontrolled postpartum bleeding can require hysterectomy when medical and conservative surgical measures fail.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Crystalloid and vasopressors cannot replace oxygen-carrying capacity or clotting factors in massive obstetric hemorrhage.
Observed shock makes immediate IV access, fluids, blood activation, and critical-care response more important.

side_effects.interpretation: Over-resuscitation can worsen pulmonary edema, especially with preeclampsia or renal impairment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Restores maternal perfusion during abruption hemorrhage while delivery/source control and coagulopathy correction are arranged.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Red-cell transfusion requires product availability or emergency-release blood.
Severe anemia or massive ongoing blood loss increases oxygen-delivery benefit.

side_effects.interpretation: Transfusion reactions are uncommon but possible during rapid blood product support.

treatments.context_specific_role: Improves oxygen delivery in maternal hemorrhage and massive transfusion pathways; does not remove the placental bleeding source.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Low fibrinogen is a key correctable driver of obstetric bleeding.
Coagulation support depends on plasma, cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen concentrate, or platelets being available.

side_effects.interpretation: Large-volume plasma can contribute to volume overload.

treatments.context_specific_role: Corrects the coagulopathy vector during abruption hemorrhage and delivery; must be paired with control of ongoing placental bleeding.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Very low platelet count increases operative and postpartum bleeding risk.
Platelet transfusion requires available components.

side_effects.interpretation: Platelet transfusion can cause febrile, allergic, or other transfusion reactions.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporarily raises platelet hemostatic capacity when DIC, bleeding, or operative delivery thresholds require it.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active maternal or fetal compromise increases value of source removal by delivery.
Previable gestation changes fetal outcome goals but does not remove maternal source-control logic when maternal risk is high.
Delivery may still be necessary, but hemorrhage risk rises when blood products are limited.

side_effects.interpretation: Delivery before term transfers risk to prematurity and neonatal support axes.
Abruption and DIC create high postpartum hemorrhage readiness needs.

treatments.context_specific_role: Removes the placenta and stops ongoing placental bed separation as a disease driver; route and timing emerge from maternal stability, fetal status, gestational age, and feasibility axes.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Viable fetal distress increases value of rapid operative delivery if maternal condition permits.
DIC and low fibrinogen increase operative bleeding toxicity and require simultaneous correction.
Absent surgical/anesthesia access or extreme instability delays or blocks operative delivery.

side_effects.interpretation: Surgery during coagulopathy can amplify maternal bleeding risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapid operative delivery vector when fetal rescue or maternal deterioration requires the shortest feasible route, with coagulopathy and blood availability strongly modulating risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Stable mother, reassuring fetal status or fetal demise, favorable labor, and no previa increase feasibility.
Placenta previa must be excluded before digital cervical exams or planned vaginal management.
A viable fetus with persistent nonreassuring status may not tolerate slow labor.

side_effects.interpretation: If delivery is slow while abruption continues, fetal hypoxia can worsen.

treatments.context_specific_role: Vaginal route vector for source control when maternal condition, fetal status, and labor context support it.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Persistent fetal compromise is not a stable monitoring-only state.
Maternal instability requires resuscitation and delivery/source control rather than expectant management.
Preterm gestation increases potential value of time when mother and fetus are stable.

side_effects.interpretation: Delay is hazardous if abruption activity accelerates despite initial stability.

treatments.context_specific_role: Observation vector for mild, stable, preterm abruption with reassuring fetal status and immediate capacity to escalate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Preterm gestation with likely delivery increases fetal lung-maturation relevance.
Immediate delivery may not allow time for full fetal corticosteroid benefit.

side_effects.interpretation: Antenatal corticosteroids can increase maternal glucose.

treatments.context_specific_role: Modifies fetal prematurity risk when stable enough to gain time; does not reshape the abruption mechanism.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Very preterm delivery context increases fetal neuroprotection relevance.
Renal impairment raises magnesium accumulation risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Magnesium can modestly lower blood pressure or worsen weakness at toxic levels.

treatments.context_specific_role: Fetal neuroprotection vector for impending very preterm delivery; not a maternal abruption treatment.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: RhD immune globulin prevents alloimmunization only in RhD-negative unsensitized patients.
No benefit when the mother is RhD-positive or already sensitized.

side_effects.interpretation: Local reaction or mild systemic symptoms can occur.

treatments.context_specific_role: Prevents Rh alloimmunization after antepartum bleeding; it does not change acute abruption, fetal hypoxia, or maternal hemorrhage dynamics.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises recurrence prior and should increase surveillance for bleeding, pain, fetal growth restriction, and fetal distress.
Placental vascular disease and high-pressure stress increase abruption prior and can coexist with HELLP/DIC physiology.
Mechanical shear between elastic uterus and less elastic placenta can trigger acute abruption after blunt trauma.
Vasospasm and hypertensive surges increase acute placental bed vessel rupture risk.
Smoking is associated with placental vascular pathology and abruption risk.
Sudden loss of uterine volume after membrane rupture, polyhydramnios decompression, or delivery of a first twin can shear placenta from the uterine wall.
Membrane rupture, inflammation, and decompression are associated with abruption and preterm delivery.
Thrombotic or malperfusion placental disease raises abruption, fetal growth restriction, and fetal compromise context.
Raises vascular and obstetric risk context but is nonspecific.
Does not create the placental separation by itself, but amplifies bleeding severity and transfusion/coagulation needs once abruption occurs.

supportive_care: Time-stamp bleeding onset, pain onset, fetal movement, trauma or decompression context, vital signs, fetal tracing, and all resuscitation steps.
Do not use normal ultrasound to exclude abruption; consume imaging hematoma axes when present but keep clinical, coagulation, and fetal-monitoring axes active.
Rule out placenta previa before digital cervical examination or planned vaginal management when the placental location is not already known.
Trend CBC, fibrinogen, PT/INR, aPTT, D-dimer or fibrin split products, lactate, creatinine, urine output, and blood product use during active bleeding.
Activate obstetric hemorrhage, anesthesia, blood bank, neonatal, and intensive-care pathways early when bleeding, shock, DIC, fetal distress, or preterm delivery risk is present.
Model DIC as vector-field superposition with D-DIC when overt consumptive coagulopathy dominates; avoid double-counting the same fibrinogen, platelet, PT/aPTT, and bleeding axes.
Keep fetal demise and fetal hypoxia as event hazards, not as the maternal lifespan outcome; maternal outcome remains mortality_hazard_in_D-PLACENTAL-ABRUPTION.
Abruption can be revealed, concealed, acute, chronic, marginal, central, partial, or complete; these are mechanism/axis contexts inside this leaf, not separate first-layer disease names.
Treatment response should emerge from delivery/source-control feasibility, maternal stability, fetal status, gestational age, coagulopathy, and blood-product axes, not from hand-written route labels.
After delivery, continue monitoring for postpartum hemorrhage, DIC rebound, renal injury, transfusion complications, and neonatal hypoxia or anemia.
